learnings.title: The 1-Day Plan
learnings.answer:
**Interview: tomorrow morning. Today: ~8 focused hours. Tomorrow: ~45 minutes.**

You are not learning new things today. You are converting what you already know into *recall under pressure*, and patching four holes. Everything below names the exact section and id to open, so you never spend a minute deciding what to study next.

> Star this entry. It is your only navigation surface today.

## Why this order

Hardest and weakest first, while attention is freshest. DSA is 30% of the expected weighting and the thinnest part of this app — it gets the first two blocks. JavaScript is your strongest pillar and already has ~180 entries here, so it gets a maintenance block near the end, not a study block.

## Today

### Block 1 — DSA patterns · 90 min

Open [/algorithm/3](/algorithm/3) and read ids **3 → 10** in order:

| id | Pattern |
| --- | --- |
| [3](/algorithm/3) | Two Pointers |
| [4](/algorithm/4) | Sliding Window |
| [5](/algorithm/5) | HashMap & Set Counting |
| [6](/algorithm/6) | Stack & Queue |
| [7](/algorithm/7) | Binary Search |
| [8](/algorithm/8) | Linked Lists |
| [9](/algorithm/9) | Trees |
| [10](/algorithm/10) | String Patterns |

**Then close the app** and hand-write, from memory, on paper or in a blank file:

1. The two-pointer converging skeleton
2. The variable-size sliding window skeleton
3. The binary search skeleton with the `left <= right` boundary

If you cannot reproduce all three cold, re-read only those and try again. This is the single highest-value 20 minutes in the day — templates you can type without thinking are what buy you time to *talk* during a live round.

### Block 2 — DSA drills, timed · 60 min

Open [/coding/39](/coding/39) and work **39 → 48**. **12 minutes each, hard stop.** Set a timer. On timeout, move on — do not reveal the solution yet.

| id | Drill | Pattern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [39](/coding/39) | `curry` | closures |
| [40](/coding/40) | Two Sum | hashmap |
| [41](/coding/41) | Longest Substring Without Repeating | sliding window |
| [42](/coding/42) | Valid Parentheses | stack |
| [43](/coding/43) | Binary Search | binary search |
| [44](/coding/44) | Reverse Linked List | pointers |
| [45](/coding/45) | Level Order Traversal | BFS |
| [46](/coding/46) | Group Anagrams | hashmap |
| [47](/coding/47) | Merge Intervals | sort + sweep |
| [48](/coding/48) | Move Zeroes | two pointers |

Only after all ten attempts, go back and read the solutions for the ones you missed. Reading a solution you never struggled against teaches almost nothing.

### Break · 30 min

Away from the screen. Walk. This is load-bearing — the next block needs a fresh head.

### Block 3 — React internals · 75 min

You said hooks are solid and internals are not, so **skip every hooks-basics entry**. Read in this order:

1. [/react-guide/2](/react-guide/2) — Elements → Fiber → DOM: the three trees
2. [/react-guide/3](/react-guide/3) — The render → commit → effects pipeline
3. [/react-guide/4](/react-guide/4) — Reconciliation: diffing by heuristic
4. [/react-guide/14](/react-guide/14) — What actually triggers a re-render
5. [/react-guide/15](/react-guide/15) — `React.memo` and the reference trap
6. [/react-guide/16](/react-guide/16) — Virtualizing big lists
7. [/react-guide/18](/react-guide/18) — "The app is slow" — the interview playbook
8. [/advanced-react/1](/advanced-react/1) — Re-renders: the myth and the mechanism
9. [/advanced-react/5](/advanced-react/5) — Mastering memoization
10. [/advanced-react/6](/advanced-react/6) — Diffing, reconciliation, and `key`
11. [/advanced-react/10](/advanced-react/10) — Closures in React: the trap and the escape hatch

Then self-quiz — **cover the answers** — on [/react-guide/37](/react-guide/37) (Gotcha Bank) and [/react-guide/38](/react-guide/38) (Rapid-Fire Q&A).

Finish with the two state-management entries, since machine-coding rounds often hand you Redux: [/react-learnings/26](/react-learnings/26) and [/react-learnings/27](/react-learnings/27).

### Block 4 — Browser & architecture · 75 min

This is the pillar with the least existing coverage and it shows up in almost every reported panel. New entries:

1. [/browser/154](/browser/154) — Critical rendering path & SPA bootstrapping
2. [/browser/155](/browser/155) — Layout / paint / composite
3. [/browser/156](/browser/156) — CORS
4. [/browser/157](/browser/157) — HTTP caching
5. [/browser/158](/browser/158) — Auth & security
6. [/browser/159](/browser/159) — Frontend API architecture
7. [/react-learnings/28](/react-learnings/28) — Scalable React architecture

Plus two you already have: [/css/6](/css/6) (reflow vs repaint, Tekion notes) and [/react-guide/29](/react-guide/29) (CSR / SSR / SSG / ISR).

**The one question to be ready for:** *"You type a URL and hit enter — walk me through everything until the page is interactive."* That single answer touches DNS, TCP/TLS, HTML parsing, the critical rendering path, bundle execution, hydration, and first data fetch. Rehearse it out loud once. It is the most-asked browser question in the reports for this level.

### Break · 30 min

### Block 5 — JavaScript rapid recall · 60 min

Maintenance, not learning. JS is your strongest pillar.

- 30 min: [/output](/output) — 20 questions on a timer. Say the answer out loud *before* you type it.
- 30 min: [/mcq](/mcq) in **Practice weak topics** mode.

If you find yourself getting a whole topic wrong, note it — do not detour into it. Note it for the morning pass.

### Block 6 — Rehearsal, out loud · 45 min

**This is the highest-leverage block in the day.** Everything above is input; this is the only output practice, and the interview is entirely output.

1. Intro script ([/interview-prep/3](/interview-prep/3)) — say it three times. Time it. It must land between 60 and 90 seconds.
2. The four-level drill ([/interview-prep/2](/interview-prep/2)) — spoken aloud, no notes, on exactly three topics: **debounce**, **`Promise.all`**, and **"the React app is slow."**

Record yourself on your phone for one of them and listen back. It is uncomfortable and it is the fastest correction loop that exists.

### Block 7 — Soft prep · 30 min

- Read [/interview-prep/4](/interview-prep/4) and settle your AI-tooling answer. The JD is explicit about this — a vague answer here is a real miss.
- Skim [/interview-prep/5](/interview-prep/5) (machine coding playbook).
- Pick three questions from [/interview-prep/7](/interview-prep/7) to ask the panel.
- Skim [/interview-prep/8](/interview-prep/8) (recovery lines) once. You want these available, not memorized.

## Tomorrow morning · 45 min

**No new material. None.** Adding input on the morning of degrades recall of everything else.

1. [/interview-prep/6](/interview-prep/6) — the cheat sheet, twice through.
2. Your **starred** items across every section — that is your personal weak list.
3. The intro script once, out loud.
4. Close the laptop 20 minutes before. Go in with a quiet head.

## If you fall behind

Drop in this order — the last item is the one you protect:

1. Block 7 (soft prep) — read it on your phone at breakfast instead
2. Block 5 (JS recall) — it is your strongest pillar
3. Half of Block 4 — keep CORS and the rendering path, drop the rest
4. **Never drop Block 6.** Speaking practice is the thing nothing else in this app trains.

learnings.title: The Four-Level Drill Protocol
60-90 Second Introduction
learnings.answer:
**Target: 60–90 seconds.** Longer and you lose the room; shorter and you've given them nothing to ask about.

Blind interview, so: no employer names you'd rather not disclose, no location, no personal details, no current-salary bait. Experience, stack, problems solved. That's it.

## The structure

Four beats. Roughly 15–20 seconds each.

1. **Who you are, professionally** — years, focus
2. **Your stack** — concrete, current
3. **One project, with a problem and an outcome** — this is the beat that matters
4. **What you're looking for** — one sentence, forward-looking

## The template

Fill the blanks, then say it until it stops sounding memorized.

> "I'm a frontend engineer with **[X]** years of experience, mostly building **[data-heavy dashboards / customer-facing product UI / internal tooling]** in React.
>
> Day to day I work in **React with JavaScript**, **[TypeScript / Redux / React Query]** for state, and I'm comfortable across the stack from **component architecture down to browser performance work**.
>
> The project I'd point to is **[project]** — **[one sentence on what it does]**. The interesting problem there was **[the actual technical problem]**. I **[what you did]**, which **[measurable or concrete outcome]**.
>
> Recently I've been going deeper on **[React internals and rendering performance / frontend architecture]**, and I'm looking for a role where I can work on **[product surface / scale / problem type]** with a team that takes engineering quality seriously."

## A worked version

> "I'm a frontend engineer with a little over two years of experience, mostly building data-heavy product UI in React.
>
> My day-to-day stack is React and JavaScript, with Redux for shared state, and I've spent a lot of time on the performance side — profiling re-renders, virtualizing large lists, and cutting bundle size.
>
> The project I'd point to is a dashboard that rendered a few thousand rows with live filtering. It was janky on every keystroke. I profiled it, found we were re-rendering the whole table on each character because the filter state lived at the top and the row components were taking fresh callback props every render. I moved the input state down, memoized the row props properly, and virtualized the list — interaction went from visibly stuttering to smooth.
>
> Lately I've been going deeper on React internals — reconciliation, the render-commit pipeline — and on browser performance more broadly. I'm looking for a role with real frontend complexity and a team that cares about how the code is built, not just that it ships."

## Why beat 3 carries the weight

**Problem → what you did → outcome.** That shape is what makes an intro memorable, and it hands the panel their next question. Almost every follow-up will come from that beat, which means *you choose what they ask you about*. Pick a project where you are strong three questions deep.

Prepare for exactly these follow-ups on whatever project you name:

- "How did you profile it?"
- "Why did that fix work?"
- "What would you do differently now?"
- "What was the hardest part?"

If any of those makes you uncomfortable, pick a different project. You have time to switch today; you won't tomorrow.

## Delivery

- **Say it out loud, three times, timed.** Silent reading does not transfer to speech. This is the single most-skipped and highest-return prep step there is.
- Slow down more than feels natural. Nervousness compresses speech, and compressed speech reads as nervous.
- Land the last sentence and **stop.** Do not trail off into "…yeah, so, that's basically me." Silence after a clean finish is confident; filler undoes the whole thing.
- Have a 20-second version too, for when they say "briefly."

## Do not

- Recite your resume chronologically — they have it
- Open with an apology or "I'm not sure where to start"
- Name technologies you can't be questioned on
- Run past 90 seconds. If you're at 2 minutes, cut beat 2 to a single clause.

learnings.title: AI Tooling Talking Points
learnings.answer:
The JD is explicit about AI tooling, which means this is a **scored question**, not small talk. Two failure modes, both common:

- **Over-claiming** — "AI writes most of my code" reads as someone who doesn't review output.
- **Dismissing** — "I prefer to write everything myself" reads as someone who won't adopt the team's workflow.

The answer they want is: *fluent user, with judgment about where it fails.*

## The shape of a strong answer

> "I use it as a fast pair, not an oracle. It's genuinely good at **[X]**, it's unreliable at **[Y]**, and here's how I verify **[Z]**."

Specificity is the whole game. Name the tool, name the task, name the check.

## Where it actually helps — pick the ones true for you

- **Scaffolding and boilerplate** — a new component with props, types, and tests wired up; a form with validation. Structure you'd write anyway, faster.
- **Unfamiliar API surface** — getting oriented in a library you haven't used, without a documentation tab-hunt.
- **Test generation** — especially edge cases you didn't think of. Then you read them, because a confidently wrong test is worse than no test.
- **Refactors with a clear shape** — "convert these class components to hooks," "extract this into a custom hook." Mechanical, reviewable, verifiable.
- **Explaining unfamiliar code** — reading into a legacy module quickly.
- **Debugging as a rubber duck** — pasting an error and a stack trace to get hypotheses, which you then check yourself.

## Where you don't trust it — this is the part that scores

Say at least two of these. This is where the judgment signal is.

- **Anything security-adjacent** — auth flows, token handling, permission checks. Confidently wrong output is dangerous here in a way it isn't elsewhere.
- **Performance work** — it suggests `useMemo` everywhere. Optimization needs a profiler and a measurement, not a pattern-match.
- **Novel business logic** — it produces plausible code for rules it can't know. Requirements come from people.
- **Anything I can't review.** If a change is too large or too unfamiliar for me to read carefully, I break it up. **I don't merge code I don't understand.**
- **Version drift** — it will confidently give you an API from three major versions ago. I check against actual docs for anything I'm not fluent in.

## How you verify

- Tests, and I read the tests rather than trusting a green checkmark
- Small diffs — I ask for narrow changes so review stays possible
- Actually running it, not just reading it
- Normal code review — AI-assisted code is held to the same bar as anything else

## A ready answer

> "I use Claude Code and Cursor daily, mostly as a fast pair. It's strongest on scaffolding and mechanical refactors — a new component with tests wired up, or converting a batch of class components to hooks. It's also good at generating edge-case tests I wouldn't have thought of, though I read every one, because a confidently wrong test is worse than no test.
>
> Where I'm more careful: anything security-related, and performance work — it'll suggest wrapping everything in `useMemo`, which usually means adding cost without removing any. That needs a profiler, not a pattern.
>
> The rule I hold to is that I don't merge code I don't understand. So I keep the diffs small enough to actually review. It's made me noticeably faster at the boilerplate parts of the job, which leaves more time for the parts that are actually hard."

## If they push

**"Has it ever led you wrong?"** — Say yes, with a real example. A plausible-looking API that didn't exist, or a subtly wrong dependency array. The point of the story is *how you caught it*.

**"How would you introduce this to a team?"** — Start with the low-risk high-volume work: tests, scaffolding, documentation. Establish that AI-assisted code goes through the same review. Never let it become a way to ship code nobody has read.

learnings.title: Machine Coding Playbook
Morning-Of Cheat Sheet
Questions to Ask the Panel
learnings.answer:
Have three ready. Ask two. It is a real part of the evaluation — "no questions" reads as no interest, and generic questions read as no preparation.

The good ones share a shape: **they could only be asked by someone who intends to do the job.**

## Strong picks

**"What does the frontend architecture look like today, and what's the part you'd change if you had a free month?"**
Everyone enjoys answering this, and the answer tells you exactly what the pain is before you sign anything.

**"How does a change get from someone's laptop to production? What's the review and release process?"**
Tells you the engineering maturity. Also signals you think past the merge button.

**"How is state managed across the app — and has that held up as it's grown?"**
Directly relevant, and it opens into architecture discussion where you're strong today.

**"What does the split look like between new product work and maintaining what exists?"**
Practical, and hard to answer evasively.

**"Where does the team stand on AI tooling — is there a shared workflow, or is it per-person?"**
Given the JD emphasis, this shows engagement with something they clearly care about.

**"What would a strong first three months look like in this role?"**
Makes them describe success concretely. Their answer is your roadmap if you take the job.

**"What's the hardest technical problem the frontend team has hit this year?"**
The best question on this list when the room is technical. You'll get a real story, and often a genuinely interesting conversation that ends the interview on a high.

## Avoid

- Anything answered on the careers page or in the JD — it reads as not having read either
- Compensation and leave policy in a technical round — that's for the recruiter
- "What's the culture like?" — too vague to produce a useful answer
- More than three. You're not interviewing them yet.

## A closing move

If the conversation went well:

> "This sounds like the kind of frontend work I'm looking for. Is there anything about my background you'd want me to expand on, or any concern I can address?"

It's direct, it's confident, and occasionally it surfaces a doubt while you can still do something about it.

learnings.title: When You're Stuck - Recovery Lines
learnings.answer:
You will get stuck. Everyone does. **Being stuck is not the failure — going silent is.** The panel cannot evaluate a blank screen, so they'll assume the worst. Keep the signal flowing.

## When your mind goes blank on a concept

> "Let me think about that for a second."

Then actually take it. Two seconds of silence you *announced* reads as considered. Two seconds you didn't reads as panic.

If it doesn't come back:

> "I know this touches on **[the adjacent thing you do know]** — can I reason through it from there?"

Partial knowledge, reasoned out loud, scores far better than a confident wrong answer. And it is genuinely what the job looks like.

## When you don't know at all

> "I haven't worked with that directly. My guess would be **[reasoned guess]**, but I'd want to verify rather than tell you something wrong. Is that close?"

**Say "I don't know" cleanly when it's true.** Interviewers at this level are specifically watching for whether you'll bluff. Someone who admits a gap is someone whose "yes" can be trusted — that's the actual signal being tested.

Never invent an API name. It is instantly recognizable and it costs you more than the gap did.

## When you're stuck mid-implementation

Narrate the state of your head:

> "Okay — I have the loop, and I'm tracking the count in a map. What I'm working out is how to handle the case where **[X]**. Let me try the brute-force version first and optimize after."

**Brute force first, out loud, is always a valid move.** Say it: *"Let me get something correct on the board, then improve it."* Interviewers like this. It's how real work goes.

## When you realize you're wrong mid-sentence

> "Actually — let me correct that. I said **[X]**, but that's not right, because **[why]**. It's **[Y]**."

Catching your own error is a *positive* signal. It shows you're still checking your reasoning rather than defending a position. Do not quietly move on and hope they missed it.

## When they push back

They may be testing whether you fold, or they may be right. Distinguish:

> "Let me reconsider — you're right that **[their point]**. So the trade-off is actually **[revised view]**."

or, if you still believe it:

> "I might be missing something. My reasoning was **[reasoning]** — where does that break down?"

Both are strong. **Folding instantly** reads as no conviction. **Refusing to engage** reads as unable to take input. Asking where the reasoning breaks is the answer that works either way.

## When you're running out of time

> "I'm watching the clock — I'd rather get this working than start the next part. Sound good?"

Then, at the end:

> "With more time I'd **[the specific next three things]**."

This recovers most of the credit for anything unfinished. Always spend the last minute on it.

## When you've frozen completely

Reset out loud. There is no penalty:

> "Let me restate the problem to make sure I have it right."

Then restate it. Restating almost always shakes something loose, and it buys thirty seconds that look like diligence rather than a stall.

## The frame to hold all day

They are not trying to catch you out. They are trying to find out **what it would be like to work with you on a hard problem**. Someone who thinks out loud, admits gaps cleanly, takes input, and keeps moving is exactly what that looks like.

You know more than you'll manage to say. Slow down. Ask before you answer. Think out loud.
